pains.title: The works won't wait for disposal

pains.title: A payment terminal is sensitive media
pains.text: POS systems and terminals carry configurations, transaction records and security components. Disposing of them as ordinary scrap opens an unnecessary door.

pains.title: A hundred stores, a hundred ways to dispose

pains.consequence: Real cost: hours of rework consolidating mismatched paperwork, or admitting there is no trail.

faqTitle: What operations and expansion teams ask

faq.q: Can you keep up with a rollout schedule?
faq.a: Yes, the collection calendar is built around the rollout or refit schedule, store by store, with windows agreed at the assessment.

faq.q: How do you handle payment terminals?
faq.a: Terminals and POS systems carrying media receive the handling defined in the scope, sanitisation or destruction, with a record that forms part of the operation report.

faq.q: Do you serve stores in several cities?
faq.a: Multi-location operations are assessed according to the number of stores, logistics and schedule, with the same documentary standard across all of them.

faq.q: And the non-electronic items in the refit?
faq.a: Our scope is electrical and electronic equipment. Furniture and building waste follow other chains, and the declared scope avoids the mixing that contaminates the documentary trail.

faq.q: How does the cost work?
faq.a: Conditions depend on the number of stores, locations, volume and requirements. The technical assessment sets the model for each operation, with no promise of a free service.

painsTitle: Formatting is not sanitisation — and the difference is costly
painsSub: Data 'erased' any old way remains recoverable with a common tool.

pains.title: The formatted disk that keeps talking
pains.text: A simple format does not remove data: it removes the index. Whoever receives the machine — leasing company, buyer or recipient — can recover files with free software.
pains.consequence: Real cost: an LGPD incident with a penalty of up to 2% of turnover (capped at R$ 50 million) — born from a piece of equipment that left 'clean'.

pains.title: The leasing return that takes your data with it
pains.text: The returned machine is refurbished and goes to the next organisation. Without recorded sanitisation, your contracts and spreadsheets travel in the package.
pains.consequence: Real cost: strategic data circulating outside your control — not even counted as a detectable breach.

pains.title: The donation that becomes a headline
pains.text: Donating computers is excellent — until a piece of sensitive data turns up on the donated machine. The social gesture becomes a reputational crisis and a legal case.
pains.consequence: Real cost: the organisation's social project suspended and the brand associated with a breach — for the wrong reason.

faqTitle: What IT, security and the DPO ask

faq.q: What is the difference between sanitisation and formatting?
faq.a: Formatting removes the index of the files; the data stays on the disk and is recoverable with common tools. Sanitisation applies a documented method of logical removal to make the data unrecoverable — with a record of the process per media.

faq.q: Is the equipment still usable afterwards?
faq.a: Yes — that is the difference from physical destruction. Sanitised media stays functional, ready for leasing return, internal reuse or donation.

faq.q: And if the media is damaged or encrypted?
faq.a: The assessment identifies media where sanitisation is not technically applicable. In those cases, we recommend physical destruction, to the same standard of record-keeping.

faq.q: Does the report identify each media?
faq.a: Yes, subject to scope: the media treated appears identified in the report, with the method applied — it is the format that audits and DPOs ask for.

faq.q: Do you also collect and dispose of the equipment?
faq.a: Yes. Sanitisation can be contracted on its own or integrated with collection, disposal and documentation for the batch — inventory, MTR and CDF where applicable.
